documents.title: ASPEN Clinical Guidelines Nutrition Support Therapy in the Adult Critically Ill Patient

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Sepsis and septic shock are common reasons for admission to the intensive care unit (ICU) ( ). These conditions can potentially lead to intestinal ischemia, impaired intestinal barrier, and even dysbiosis, resulting in acute gastrointestinal injury (AGI) in critically ill patients. The Working Group on Abdominal Problems of the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM) defines AGI as gastrointestinal dysfunction due to acute illness in intensive care patients ( ). Studies have shown that critically ill patients without AGI experience lower mortality than those with AGI ( – ). Therefore, it is imperative to pay attention to the AGI in patients with sepsis. Early enteral nutrition (EN) can produce beneficial physiological effects in critically ill patients via the downregulation of systemic immune responses, reduction of oxidative stress, and maintenance of gut microecology, leading to improved patient outcomes ( – ). Some recent studies have shown that EN is associated with lower AGI grades in patients with AGI and lower mortality in patients with sepsis ( – ). Hence, EN plays a vital role in sepsis patients with AGI. In line with the 2021 international guidelines for the management of sepsis and septic shock, early initiation of EN within 72 h is recommended for adult patients with sepsis or septic shock who are suitable for enteral feeding ( ). Unfortunately, the guideline did not provide specific recommendations regarding EN formulas for patients with sepsis. Guidelines recommend the routine use of standard polymeric formulas in critically ill patients ( ). However, it remains unclear whether short-peptide formulas can leverage their pre-digested properties to reduce the burden of digestion and absorption and thereby benefit sepsis patients with AGI ( – ). Therefore, this exploratory study aimed to investigate the effects of these two EN formulas on clinical outcomes in critically ill sepsis patients with AGI grades I and II. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study design and participants We conducted a retrospective cohort study on adult patients with AGI and sepsis admitted to the ICU of our hospital (The comprehensive ICU of the third class and has a total of 56 beds in 3 treatment areas) between March 2018 and October 2023 ( ). The inclusion criteria of this study included: (1) age ≥ 18 years; (2) met the diagnostic criteria of Sepsis-3 ( ); (3) admitted to the ICU for ≥7 days; (4) AGI grades I-II (AGI grade I: risk of developing gastrointestinal dysfunction or failure; AGI grade II: gastrointestinal dysfunction) proposed by the 2012 ESICM guideline ( ); and (5) short-peptide formulas or standard-polymeric formulas used within 7 days of ICU admission. The exclusion criteria of this study were as follows: (1) received oral feeding, (2) EN was administered prior to ICU admission, (3) did not receive feeding according to nutrition protocols, (4) EN formulas cross use, (5) had participated in other similar clinical studies, (6) had malignant tumors, (7) were pregnant, (8) missed clinical data, (9) follow-up failure. According to the type of EN formulas used by critically ill patients, they were assigned to a short-peptide formulas group and a standard-polymeric formulas group. The 2018 European Society for Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism (ESPEN) guidelines divided the clinical stage of patients in the ICU into the Ebb and flow phases; the first 7 days of the flow phase are called the acute phase ( ), and the acute phase is divided into the early period (metabolic instability and severe increase in catabolism, within 48 h after injury) and late period (a significant muscle wasting and a stabilization of the metabolic disturbances, 48 h after injury). Considering the differences in the severity of severe disease, the severity of infection, and the presence or absence of shock, different EN initiation times were selected. To reduce bias due to baseline differences, we set up a subgroup analysis based on this guideline. Patients were assigned to the early EN (EEN) subgroup (those who received EN within 48 h) and delayed EN (DEN) subgroup (those who received EN within day 3–7). Different degrees of AGI were shown in , and the EN startup ratios of the EEN and DEN subgroups were shown in . In accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations, all methods employed in this retrospective cohort study were conducted in compliance with ethical standards and approved by the Ethics Committee of the First Hospital of Jilin University (No. 2022-483). methods employed in this retrospective cohort study were conducted in compliance with ethical standards and approved by the Ethics Committee of the First Hospital of Jilin University (No. 2022-483). Informed consent was waived by the Ethics Committee of the First Hospital of Jilin University for this retrospective study, as it did not involve human participants or tissue samples. 2.2 Nutrition protocols Clinicians in our department had implemented customized nutrition protocols for each severely ill AGI patient according to ESICM guidelines ( ). For example, patients with AGI grades I–II and severe disease were initiated on an EF dose of 20 mL/h ( ), with caloric and protein targets set at 25 kcal/kg/day and 1.2–2.0 g/kg/day, respectively ( ), as recommended by guidelines, actual body weight was used for patients with body mass index (BMI) < 25 kg/m 2 , whereas adjusted body weight (AdjBW) was used for BMI ≥ 25 kg/m 2 . AdjBW was calculated as ideal body weight (IBW) + 0.25 × (Actual − IBW) and that IBW was calculated as 0.9 × height (cm) − 100 for males and 0.9 × height (cm) − 106 for females ( ). Appropriate supplemental parenteral nutrition was provided if enteral routes fail to meet nutritional goals within a short timeframe. Initiating EN at a full dose at the start of feeding was prespecified as a protocol violation. Because this was a retrospective study, temporary EN dose reductions or interruptions during the subsequent course of feeding (e.g., in response to gastrointestinal symptoms or persistent shock) were considered routine clinical care and were not classified as protocol deviations. Additionally, GI symptoms are closely monitored to adjust EF dosing. Patients who had lost or did not follow their nutritional protocols were excluded from this study. The clinician selects the short-peptide formulas (1 kcaL/mL, 20 g/500 mL of protein) or standard-polymeric formulas (1.5 kcaL/mL, 30 g/500 mL of protein) according to their preference and patient’s condition. The comparison of the characteristics of the two formulas is detailed in . All patients were fed with continuous infusion. 2.3 Clinical data collection Collect patient clinical data from electronic medical records, such as primary diagnosis (most important cause or disease leading to admission to the ICU), EN initiation time, acute physiology and chronic health evaluation (APACHE) II scores, sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) scores, nutrition risk screening (NRS) scores, modified NUTRIC (mNUTRIC) scores, AGI grades, and serum albumin levels. All scores related to disease severity and nutritional status and AGI grades were calculated from the clinical data of severely ill patients within the first 24 h of ICU admission. The patients’ daily intakes of protein and calories from EN, ICU length of stay, hospital length of stay, hospitalization cost, ventilator-free days, ICU and 28-day mortality, were recorded, and adverse gastrointestinal events during their ICU stay, if it occurred, were also obtained. 2.4 Primary and secondary outcomes The primary outcomes were caloric adequacy of EN (≥80% of target calories) on day 7. The secondary outcomes were calories and protein gain from EN within 3–7 days (calories or protein fed through EN on the 7th day minus calories or protein fed through EN on the 3rd day), the incidence of gastric retention (a single volume ≥ 200 mL), and diarrhea (loose stools ≥ 3 times per day or liquid stools with a stool weight > 250 mL/day or > 200–250 g/day) ( ) after EN administration, daily caloric EN/(EN + Parenteral nutrition (PN)) ratios, ICU and 28-day mortality, ICU and hospital length of stay, ventilator-free days and hospitalization cost. 2.5 Sample size calculation To the best of our knowledge, no previous studies have directly compared short-peptide and standard polymeric formulas in sepsis patients with AGI. Based on a prior study in AGI patients ( ), we assumed probabilities of achieving 80% of the caloric target by day 7 to be 80% (short-peptide group) and 50% (standard polymeric group), with a 1:1 allocation ratio. Using these proportions, a sample size of 72 patients (36 per group) was calculated ( α = 0.05, power = 0.80) via PASS software. Because our prespecified analyses compared the two formulas separately within the EEN and DEN subgroups, the overall planned sample size was 144 patients (EEN: 72 [36 + 36]; DEN: 72 [36 + 36]). Given the exploratory nature of this study, this sample size is adequate for preliminary insights. 2.6 Statistical analysis The statistical software used was SPSS 26.0 (Armonk, NY, United States: IBM Corp). Normality of continuous variables was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test (two-sided α = 0.05) within each study group. Continuous variables are defined as mean ± standard deviation if they were normally distributed; otherwise, median values and interquartile ranges M (P25, P75) were represented. Differences between the two groups were determined using t -test for normally distributed continuous variables

Normality of continuous variables was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test (two-sided α = 0.05) within each study group. Continuous variables are defined as mean ± standard deviation if they were normally distributed; otherwise, median values and interquartile ranges M (P25, P75) were represented. Differences between the two groups were determined using t -test for normally distributed continuous variables and the Mann–Whitney U test for nonparametric data. Categorical data were compared between the two groups using the chi-square test (or Fisher’s exact test when expected counts were <5). The Spearman correlation coefficient and variance inflation factor were performed to detect collinearity among the variables. For prespecified secondary outcomes, we controlled the false discovery rate (FDR) at 5% using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure; for transparency, we report uncorrected p -values together with FDR-adjusted p -values in the . Parameters with p < 0.1 in the univariate analysis were entered into the multiple logistic regression analysis to identify the predictors for caloric adequacy of EN on day 7. The confounders considered in the multivariate regression analysis were based on the results of the univariate logistic regression for different subgroups (EEN and DEN). The confounders included in each subgroup’s multivariate logistic regression were different, as outlined in . Kaplan–Meier survival analysis was performed to estimate the 28-day cumulative survival. Statistical significance for the primary outcome was set at two-sided p < 0.05 (no multiplicity adjustment). Due to the retrospective nature of this study, significant differences in baseline characteristics between the early enteral nutrition (EEN) and delayed enteral nutrition (DEN) groups precluded their combined analysis. Therefore, we separately compared the effects of short-peptide and standard polymeric formulas within each subgroup (EEN and DEN) to explore their clinical outcomes. 3 Results 3.1 Baseline characteristics and initial severity of illness Of the 1,644 patients screened for eligibility, a total of 376 patients who met the inclusion criteria and did not meet the exclusion criteria were eventually included in the study. The number of excluded patients and the reasons are as follows: 919 patients did not fulfill the inclusion criteria, 42 patients received oral feeding, 73 patients received EN prior to ICU admission, 48 patients were cross-used EN formulations, 80 patients had participated in other similar clinical studies, 17 patients did not feeding follow the nutritional protocols (start with a full-dose feeding of 40-50 mL/h), 15 patients had malignant tumors, 43 patients were pregnant, 21 patients had missing clinical data, and 10 patients were not followed-up. Therefore, 376 patients were evaluated for the effect of the short-peptide and standard-polymeric formulas on the feeding outcome and clinical outcome of severely ill patients with sepsis and AGI grades I–II ( ). Baseline patient characteristics of the EEN and DEN subgroups are presented in . 3.2 Primary outcomes 3.2.1 Caloric adequacy In the EEN subgroup, the caloric adequacy of EN on day 7 in the short-peptide group was higher than that of the standard-polymeric group (59.1% vs. 27.3%, p = 0.001). However, in the DEN subgroup, the caloric adequacy of EN on day 7 in the short-peptide group was lower than that of the standard-polymeric group (28.6% vs. 43.5%, p = 0.02) ( and ). describe the results of the logistic regression analysis for the EEN and DEN subgroups, respectively. mNUTRIC and APACHE II scores were excluded from the multivariate analysis because of their high collinearity ( ). The short-peptide formulas were associated with EN caloric adequacy on day 7 after controlling for covariates in the EEN subgroup ( OR: 3.852, 95% CI: 1.851–8.017; p < 0.001). In addition, in the DEN subgroup, the EN caloric adequacy on day 7 associated with the standard-polymeric formulas ( OR: 2.409, 95% CI: 1.325–4.378; p = 0.004), gastric retention ( OR: 0.272, 95% CI: 0.115–0.643; p = 0.003), and diarrhea ( OR: 0.548, 95% CI: 0.378–0.796; p = 0.002). 3.3 Secondary outcomes 3.3.1 Calories and protein gain In the EEN subgroup, calories and protein gain from EN were higher in the short-peptide group than in the standard-polymeric group (624[0, 936] vs. 0[− 360, 480], p = 0.001; 24[0, 38] vs. 0[− 14.4, 19.2], p = 0.003, respectively). However, in the DEN subgroup, calories and protein gain from EN were lower in the short-peptide group than in the standard-polymeric group (960[480, 1,200] vs. 1,080[720, 1,440], p = 0.04; 38.4[19.2, 50.4] vs. 43.2[28.8, 57.6], p = 0.04, respectively) ( and ). Associations between calories/protein gain from EN within 3-7d and critical illness and clinical outcomes are presented in . 3.3.2 Adverse gastrointestinal events In the EEN subgroup, the incidence of gastric retention (18.2% vs. 36.4%,

than in the standard-polymeric group (624[0, 936] vs. 0[− 360, 480], p = 0.001; 24[0, 38] vs. 0[− 14.4, 19.2], p = 0.003, respectively). However, in the DEN subgroup, calories and protein gain from EN were lower in the short-peptide group than in the standard-polymeric group (960[480, 1,200] vs. 1,080[720, 1,440], p = 0.04; 38.4[19.2, 50.4] vs. 43.2[28.8, 57.6], p = 0.04, respectively) ( and ). Associations between calories/protein gain from EN within 3-7d and critical illness and clinical outcomes are presented in . 3.3.2 Adverse gastrointestinal events In the EEN subgroup, the incidence of gastric retention (18.2% vs. 36.4%, p = 0.03) and diarrhea (9.1% vs. 25.5%, p = 0.02) was lower in the short-peptide group than in the standard-polymeric group. However, in the DEN subgroup, there were no statistically significant differences in the incidence of gastric retention and diarrhea between the short peptide and standard polymeric groups ( p > 0.05) ( and ). 3.3.3 Daily caloric EN/(EN + PN) ratios In the EEN subgroup, caloric EN/(EN + PN) ratios were higher on day 6 and 7 in the short-peptide group than in the standard-polymeric group ( p = 0.021; p = 0.044, respectively). In the DEN subgroup, caloric EN/(EN + PN) ratios were higher on day 6 in the standard-polymeric group than in the short-peptide group ( p = 0.024) ( and ). 3.3.4 Clinical outcomes There were no statistically significant differences were observed in ICU and 28-day mortality, ICU length of stay, hospital length of stay, ventilator-free days and hospitalization cost in the short-peptide and standard-polymeric formulas group in both the EEN and DEN subgroups ( p > 0.05) ( ). Kaplan–Meier survival curves plotted with the 28-day mortality rates also did not show a statistically significant difference between the EEN ( log-rank p = 0.70) and DEN subgroups ( log-rank p = 0.33) ( ). In , we report the uncorrected and FDR-corrected p -values for all secondary outcomes to address potential issues related to multiple comparisons. 4 Discussion This study compared the effects of different EN formulas on clinical outcomes in critically ill sepsis patients with AGI grades I-II, with subgroup analysis based on the timing of EN initiation (EEN and DEN subgroups). In the EEN subgroup, the short-peptide formula resulted in higher caloric adequacy, as well as greater calorie and protein gain from EN compared to the standard-polymer group. It also showed lower incidence of gastric retention and diarrhea, along with a higher EN/(EN + PN) ratio on days 6 and 7. However, in the DEN subgroup, the standard-polymer formula had higher caloric adequacy and calorie/protein gain compared to the short-peptide formula. There were no significant differences in gastric retention or diarrhea between the two groups, but the standard-polymer group had a higher EN/(EN + PN) ratio on day 3. Both formulas showed similar outcomes in terms of ICU and hospital stay, costs, mortality, and ventilator-free days. The EEN may be beneficial for patients with sepsis and AGI (it can maintain gut integrity and prevent intestinal permeability) ( , ); however, it may also lead to intestinal ischemia and gastrointestinal adverse events, which can lead to feeding intolerance syndrome and a more severe gastrointestinal injury. The short-peptide EN formulas can be absorbed without digestive enzymes, which may reduce the incidence of intolerance and undesired gastrointestinal events in patients ( ). The short-peptide EN formulas can be digested and absorbed faster from the gut, make amino acids more available after meals, and promote the binding of dietary amino acids to skeletal muscle protein ( ). It has been shown that N -formyl-methionyl-leucyl-phenylalanine transport in the colon of rats increases the expression of oligopeptide transporter, which may damage colonic mucosa ( , ). Short-peptides can protect the intestinal mucosa and reduce intestinal damage because they can competitively inhibit N -formyl-methionyl-leucyl-phenylalanine transport or have a greater transport efficiency ( ). In the early acute phase of critical illness (≤48 h) ( ), the short-peptide formulas may be more suitable for critically ill patients with sepsis and AGI grade I than the standard-polymeric formulas. The feeding tolerance outcomes and nutritional adequacy outcomes in the EEN group support this view. Furthermore, the findings related to calorie and protein gain from EN within 3–7d remained statistically robust even after applying FDR correction. These results highlight the potential clinical significance of the observed effects and underscore the need for further validation in larger, prospective studies. Studies have showed ( ), the higher the average EN/(EN + PN) ratio of patients admitted to ICU within 7 days, the lower the in-hospital mortality. In the EEN subgroup, the short-peptide formula group had a higher EN proportion on days 6 and 7, which may indicate some potential benefits. However, no differences were found in other clinical outcomes between the two groups. These results

These results highlight the potential clinical significance of the observed effects and underscore the need for further validation in larger, prospective studies. Studies have showed ( ), the higher the average EN/(EN + PN) ratio of patients admitted to ICU within 7 days, the lower the in-hospital mortality. In the EEN subgroup, the short-peptide formula group had a higher EN proportion on days 6 and 7, which may indicate some potential benefits. However, no differences were found in other clinical outcomes between the two groups. These results are similar to those of previous studies ( , – ). According to our results, the short-peptide formulas can be considered in critically ill patients with sepsis and AGI grade I or II, if the administration of EN is started within 48 h. The DEN subgroup had a lower MAP (72.4 mmHg vs. 86.7 mmHg) and a higher percentage of primary AGI (38.7% vs. 11.7%) than the EEN subgroup. The gastrointestinal tract of patients with primary AGI may require more rest than that of patients with secondary AGI, and patients with lower MAP are at a higher risk of intestinal ischemia. We had proposed the gut rest strategy (trophic feeding after 72 h of ICU admission may be the better option for AGI patients) ( ). Therefore, it is reasonable to delay the EN start timing. In the DEN subgroup of this study, the caloric adequacy of EN on day 7, and calories and protein gain from EN within 3–d in the standard-polymeric group was higher. This unexpected result seems difficult to explain, especially since the incidence of gastric retention and diarrhea was similar between the two groups. One possible reason for this outcome could be the difference in energy density between the two EN formulas (short-peptide formula 1.0 kcaL/mL vs. standard polymer formula 1.5 kcaL/mL), making it easier for the standard polymer group to achieve nutritional goals. In the late acute phase of critical illness (˃48 h) ( ), metabolic function and gastrointestinal digestion and absorption function were gradually recovered in critically ill patients. The gastrointestinal blood flow and permeability were improved, the digestive system had a good rest ( ), and the tolerance of the gastrointestinal tract might be stronger. In this case, the disadvantage of short peptides is magnified, and this advantage is difficult to achieve. Therefore, the standard-polymeric formulas may be considered for critically ill patients with sepsis and AGI grades I–II if EN administration starts after 48 h. Unfortunately, in the DEN group, there was no statistical difference in all secondary outcomes after FDR adjustment. An interesting problem was found in this study: in the DEN subgroup, the standard-polymeric formulas was associated with caloric adequacy of EN on day 7; however, diarrhea and gastric retention were also associated with EN caloric adequacy on day 7. This is because, based on late initiation of EN, it is more difficult to reach caloric adequacy of EN on day 7 if diarrhea and gastric retention occur. The relatively small sample size of the short-peptide group in the EEN subgroup may represent an interesting issue. One possible explanation for this observation is that clinicians who prefer short-peptide formulas may be more inclined to delay EN initiation when managing sepsis patients with AGI, potentially due to concerns about gastrointestinal tolerance or other clinical considerations. In addition, in the correlation analysis of the calories/protein gain from EN within 3-7d with critical illness and clinical outcomes, it can be found that the nutritional increase in the EEN group is associated with the nutritional formula and APACHE II score > 15, while in the DEN group it is associated with MAP and gastrointestinal symptoms. It may be indicated that there are differences between the EEN group and the DEN group. This exploratory result requires careful interpretation. This study had some limitations. First, this study is retrospective in design and therefore inherently subject to selection bias. The clinicians’ choice of nutritional formulas represents the most significant source of such bias. Additionally, the imbalance between groups could have contributed to residual bias, leading to a selection bias. Although baseline characteristics were relatively balanced between the two formula groups across subgroups, it should be acknowledged that the short-peptide group exhibited higher rates of nasojejunal tube utilization and a greater proportion of primary AGI cases. These limitations are inherent to retrospective studies and underscore the need for prospective investigations to validate our findings. Second, the caloric target was calculated with an equation rather than indirect calorimetry, which may affect the accuracy of the caloric goal calculation. Third, we were unable to draw evidence-based conclusions regarding when EN should be initiated for patients with sepsis and AGI grades I–II because of uneven baselines in the two parts (the

two formula groups across subgroups, it should be acknowledged that the short-peptide group exhibited higher rates of nasojejunal tube utilization and a greater proportion of primary AGI cases. These limitations are inherent to retrospective studies and underscore the need for prospective investigations to validate our findings. Second, the caloric target was calculated with an equation rather than indirect calorimetry, which may affect the accuracy of the caloric goal calculation. Third, we were unable to draw evidence-based conclusions regarding when EN should be initiated for patients with sepsis and AGI grades I–II because of uneven baselines in the two parts (the provision of EN within 48 h and the provision of EN after 48 h). Fourth, this study only included patients with AGI grades I–II, which would limit the extrapolation of these exploratory findings. Finally, the relatively small and unbalanced sample size, especially in the EEN subgroup, which may affect the generalizability and reliability of the results. Although the sample size exceeded the calculated requirement, it must be acknowledged that these exploratory results may lack robustness. However, this was the first study to explore the impact of short-peptide and standard-polymeric EN formulas on feeding and clinical outcomes on severe sepsis patients with AGI. Further randomized control trials are required to confirm the results of our study. 5 Conclusion In this retrospective exploratory cohort of sepsis patients with AGI grades I-II, preliminary findings observed that short-peptide formulas may be considered for those who initiate EN early (≤48 h), while standard-polymer formulas may be an option for those who initiate EN late (>48 h). These observations did not translate into differences in hard outcomes and should be regarded as hypothesis-generating. Prospective, adequately powered studies are needed before any practice implications can be drawn.

documents.title: ASPEN Parenteral Nutrition Safety Consensus Recommendations

chunks.content: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS A structured quality improvement initiative with checklists, designated personnel and routine surveillance improved adherence to standardised TPN preparation and administration. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY This pragmatic, process-driven model offers a scalable approach to strengthen adherence to standardised TPN practices and can inform future research, clinical practice and policy. Introduction Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) is essential for neonates who cannot meet their nutritional needs enterally due to gastrointestinal immaturity or dysfunction. The primary goal is to prevent growth faltering while ensuring safe, effective nutritional support through careful monitoring and adjustments based on clinical status. Despite its necessity, TPN is complex and requiring expertise at every stage. Variability in TPN practices is driven by limited high-quality evidence, resource constraints and outdated protocols, often resulting in inadequate nutrition and poor growth outcomes. Neonates are particularly vulnerable to adverse events due to both the therapy itself and its intricate multistep process. Variations in healthcare settings and stakeholder practices contribute to inconsistencies in parenteral nutrition (PN) prescription, preparation and administration. Local problem Despite the benefits of standardised TPN practices, our neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) struggled with adherence to optimal preparation and monitoring protocols. In our 60-bed tertiary NICU, admitting ~1500 neonates annually, TPN preparation was inconsistent due to variability in technique, sterility and adherence to guidelines. Initially, suboptimal formulations were prepared by nursing staff. TPN components were often prepared separately at the bedside and at different times for each baby, rather than in one coordinated session. This unmonitored process led to inconsistent preparation, unnecessary wastage of ingredients and increased infection risk. Instead of a single compounded solution, amino acids, lipids and dextrose-electrolyte solutions were often administered separately, increasing contamination risk due to multiple connections. During a sepsis outbreak, review of infection control practices revealed the absence of a formal laminar flow surveillance system. Although the outbreak was not linked to TPN, this gap highlighted the need for routine monitoring. Additionally, compliance with TPN preparation protocols was only ~10% in the 4 months preceding the quality improvement (QI) project (January–April 2024), underscoring the need for structured improvements. Available knowledge PN practices for newborns and preterm infants vary globally due to differences in prescription, preparation and administration. Despite established guidelines, adherence remains inconsistent, especially in resource-limited settings where cost, availability and lack of trained personnel are major barriers. In developed countries, PN is prepared by trained pharmacists under strict aseptic conditions, while in India and other developing nations, it is often manually compounded by physicians and nurses, increasing risks of contamination and errors. Structured training, improved monitoring and proactive PN strategies have been shown to enhance outcomes in preterm infants. In South Africa, standardised ‘all-in-one’ PN bags have been proposed for facilities without pharmacy units, while Egypt’s educational programmes improved PN practices. Kuwait highlighted the role of multidisciplinary teams, regular audits and standard protocols. PN prescribing errors, often due to non-standardised orders and miscommunication, can be reduced by standardised forms, multidisciplinary review and computerised order entry. Compounding under laminar flow hoods and using automated compounding devices improve safety and accuracy, though verification remains crucial. These findings stress the need for structured PN programmes, enhanced training and improved implementation in resource-limited settings. Rationale We applied the WHO Point of Care QI framework to address the problem of low adherence to existing TPN protocols in our NICU. Although standardised protocols were available, daily practice showed wide variation due to unclear responsibilities, lack of structured training and absence of routine monitoring. We believed that simple, practical interventions—such as defining roles, providing targeted training and regularly reviewing practice—would improve adherence. The approach focused on making changes that were feasible, sustainable and easily integrated into the existing workflow. SMART aim (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound aim) To improve compliance with standardised TPN preparation and administration protocols in the NICU from a baseline of approximately 10% to at least 80% within an 8-month period, by implementing structured interventions including centralised preparation, staff training, protocol standardisation and routine process monitoring—ensuring measurable and sustainable improvements in safety and quality. Setting The study was conducted in a 60-bed, Level IIIB accredited NICU of a tertiary care teaching hospital, with~1500 annual admissions. Of these, 20 beds cater to Level IIIB care. The unit is staffed by five consultants and a total of 15 neonatology residents, with per-shift coverage including 5–7 nurses and 3–5 residents, varying depending on census and acuity. The unit has a designated TPN preparation room with a laminar airflow workstation to enable aseptic compounding. Although standardised TPN protocols (eg, National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) 2020 guidelines and the European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition (ESPGHAN) 2018 recommendations) existed, adherence was low, leading to inconsistencies in preparation and administration. Intervention Patients were

with~1500 annual admissions. Of these, 20 beds cater to Level IIIB care. The unit is staffed by five consultants and a total of 15 neonatology residents, with per-shift coverage including 5–7 nurses and 3–5 residents, varying depending on census and acuity. The unit has a designated TPN preparation room with a laminar airflow workstation to enable aseptic compounding. Although standardised TPN protocols (eg, National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) 2020 guidelines and the European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition (ESPGHAN) 2018 recommendations) existed, adherence was low, leading to inconsistencies in preparation and administration. Intervention Patients were assessed for TPN eligibility based on standard clinical indications such as prematurity, surgical conditions, feed intolerance or critical illness. Eligibility was determined according to unit protocols, in line with international guidelines including NICE (2020), ESPGHAN (2018) and the National Neonatology Forum recommendations. A QI initiative using planning, implementation, evaluation and action (PDSA) cycles was implemented to improve adherence to standardised TPN protocols. Gap analysis ( ) identified key issues: inconsistent preparation techniques, inadequate training and contamination risks. Interventions were implemented sequentially through PDSA cycles, targeting preparation practices, calculation errors, sterility and workflow (details in the PDSA section). The team included neonatologists (protocol development, supervision), residents and fellows (TPN preparation, adherence monitoring), NICU nursing staff (workflow integration) and infection control personnel (sterilisation compliance). Regular team meetings facilitated continuous evaluation. A process mapping exercise ( ) helped optimise workflow. The project was planned for months, allowing for ongoing assessment and continuous refinement of interventions. Patient and public involvement No patients were involved. TPN administration to eligible neonates is standard of care, and this project focused on improving internal NICU processes for its prescribing, compounding and administration. Study of the intervention A pre-intervention and post-intervention analysis assessed adherence to protocols, formulation accuracy and preparation compliance. Data from audits and observations were analysed using PDSA cycles, with feedback sessions to address confounders. Comparisons with past NICU data ensured improvements were intervention-driven. PDSA cycles For each PDSA cycle, we explicitly describe the planning, implementation, evaluation and actions taken for sustainability, summarised in . PDSA cycle 1: transitioning TPN preparation to residents and fellows Though standard guidelines for TPN existed (NICE 2020, ESPGHAN 2018), they did not specifically address preparation and administration practices. In our unit, considerable inconsistencies were observed in these processes, and baseline adherence was only 10%. The first step was to formulate a structured unit protocol for TPN preparation and administration that detailed who would prepare TPN (trained residents and fellows instead of nurses), how it would be prepared (under a UV-exposed laminar flow hood using a standardised 11-step checklist and individualised formulations, with amino acids mixed with dextrose-electrolyte solutions and lipids administered separately) and when it would be prepared (once daily in a coordinated session). A structured training programme was delivered through hands-on demonstrations, video tutorials and written guides; this was conducted in two batches to accommodate clinical duties, with monthly reinforcement sessions for residents and Level III nurses. Adherence was assessed using the 11-step checklist ( ), which covered eligibility, preparation, labelling and administration steps and was completed through direct observation with real-time feedback. Within 2 weeks, adherence improved to 79%, accompanied by better workflow efficiency, reduced preparation time and greater acceptance of the protocol. The intervention was subsequently adopted into routine practice, supported by ongoing education and continuous monitoring. PDSA cycle 2: introduction of TPN calculator Manual TPN calculations often led to inconsistencies and potential errors. To standardise formulations and improve accuracy, an Excel-based TPN calculator was developed. Following structured training, residents and fellows used the tool during a 2-week testing phase for daily TPN preparation. Protocol adherence improved from 76.7% in week 3 to 85.7% in week 4. The calculator enhanced dosage accuracy, minimised calculation errors and increased user confidence. Based on these positive outcomes, it was integrated into routine practice, with periodic updates planned based on user feedback. PDSA cycle 3: laminar flow surveillance and contamination prevention A sepsis outbreak during the early phase of the project (week 5 and 6) led to a review of infection control practices, revealing the absence of a structured laminar flow surveillance system. Although unrelated to TPN, this prompted a temporary 2-week halt in TPN preparation. A comprehensive surveillance protocol was introduced, including routine cleaning, biweekly surface cultures, monthly air quality monitoring and biannual High-Efficiency Particulate Air (HEPA) filter integrity checks ( ). Staff were trained on environmental hygiene, and adherence improved within a week, reaching 100% in week 7. The protocol was integrated into routine practice with regular audits and ongoing education to minimise contamination risks. PDSA cycle 4: implementing a computerised TPN prescription template Handwritten TPN prescriptions often led to transcription errors, resulting in delays as parents were repeatedly sent back to the NICU for corrections; this disrupted workflow and contributed to a decline in adherence to 78.9% in week 11. To address these issues, a standardised computerised prescription template was introduced, aiming to enhance accuracy, streamline workflow and ensure documentation consistency. After a 2-week testing phase and refinements based on user feedback, adherence improved significantly, reaching 100% by week 13. The intervention was successfully integrated into routine practice, with provisions for ongoing evaluation and updates. PDSA cycle 5: TPN preparation rotation schedule Although adherence had improved significantly—exceeding 90% in weeks 14 and 19, and reaching 100% in weeks 16–18—a drop to 86.2% in week 20, though within the SMART aim, highlighted workflow inefficiencies from preparation delays and lack of designated personnel. To address this and ensure reliability, a structured rotation schedule was introduced, assigning clear roles and incorporating backup personnel for uninterrupted workflow. Over 2 weeks, this intervention improved coordination, minimised delays and stabilised processes, with adherence rebounding to 100% in week 23. Owing to its success, the schedule was adopted into routine practice with ongoing monitoring. A financial concern was raised by the nursing in-charge about the daily preparation of fresh TPN, involving individual prescriptions and potentially higher patient costs. To address this, we undertook a crude comparison of the prices of key consumables (drip sets, electrolytes, multivitamins, amino acids, dextrose, lipids, syringes, needles, etc) before and after the intervention, per patient, which did not show any appreciable difference from previous practices. In addition, TPN for all eligible babies was prepared together, enabling shared use of components and rotating prescriptions. Tested over 2 weeks, this approach improved efficiency and managed costs effectively. Based on positive feedback, the strategy was integrated into routine practice to reduce financial strain while maintaining TPN quality. PDSA cycle 6: inventory management system To prevent TPN preparation delays due to shortage of supply, an inventory management system was introduced to track stock levels and automate reordering. A 2-week trial assessed its effectiveness, with real-time inventory tracking and team training. However, technical difficulties, stock discrepancies and increased workload disrupted workflow, leading to overordering and shortages. Due to these challenges, the system was discontinued, and manual tracking resumed while alternative management solutions were explored. In week 25, adherence declined to 86.7%, and 2 out of 15 opportunities halted within 6 hours due to metabolic instability. To address this, TPN formulations were proactively modified using prior patient data to anticipate common derangements and improve tolerance in this vulnerable group. Within 2 weeks, adherence improved and remained consistently above the SMART aim, including 100% adherence in weeks 28 and 30. The revised strategy was integrated into routine practice, with ongoing data-driven refinements to ensure continued safety and efficacy in ELBW infants. Measures Outcome measures The primary outcome was adherence to standardised TPN preparation and administration, defined as the percentage of TPN preparations meeting protocol requirements. Adherence was assessed using an 11-step process checklist covering eligibility assessment, order calculation, prescription, preparation, aseptic precautions, labelling, administration and waste disposal ( ). Each step was scored as ‘done’ (yes) or ‘not done’ (no). Each TPN preparation was considered ‘adherent’ only if all 11 steps were performed correctly (all scored as ‘yes’). Weekly adherence was then calculated as the proportion of fully adherent TPN preparations among all eligible preparations. The goal was to improve adherence to TPN protocols from a baseline of 10% to over 80%, aiming to bring more consistency to the preparation process and strengthen overall quality of care. Data were collected through direct observation, periodic audits and documentation reviews. Historical data were analysed to confirm that improvements were due to interventions rather than other NICU practice changes. The primary focus of this initiative was on process improvement. While overall sepsis incidence among inborn neonates on TPN was reviewed as a balancing measure, specific Central Line–Associated Bloodstream Infection (CLABSI) rates could not be calculated since central line tip cultures are not routinely performed. Process measures Two key process measures were tracked. First, the transition of TPN preparation from neonatal nursing staff to trained residents and fellows was assessed by monitoring the percentage of TPN preparations performed by trained personnel and the number of completed training sessions. Competency assessments and audits ensured accuracy and adherence to protocols. Second, laminar flow surveillance consistency was evaluated through routine sterility audits and microbiological testing. The rate of detected contamination in TPN preparations was used to measure the impact of enhanced surveillance. Ambiguous steps identified in the baseline process map ( ) included the review of appropriateness of calculations (later standardised by incorporating routine discussion of eligibility and composition during clinical rounds), placement of components on the laminar hood surface after disinfection (addressed through structured cleaning protocols and checklist steps) and switching on of the fan filter unit (made reliable through checklist integration and direct observation). Assessment approach A structured evaluation framework led by the senior resident involved regular audits and competency assessments to ensure adherence to TPN protocols. Real-time feedback enabled prompt correction of procedural lapses. Residents and fellows received standardised training from a neonatologist using evidence-based protocols, reading material and instructional videos. Laminar flow integrity was tracked via a dedicated log reviewed by the infection control nurse, sister-in-charge, and senior resident, enabling early breach detection. Periodic review meetings discussed findings, challenges, and action plans, promoting accountability and continuous improvement. This approach strengthened protocol compliance and enhanced the safety and reliability of TPN administration in the NICU. Analysis Statistical analysis used run and p charts to track adherence to standardised TPN protocols over time. Laminar flow surveillance, a key process measure, was evaluated using run charts (performed vs not performed). P chart analysis in R software (V.4.3.1, R Core Team, 2023) confirmed all points remained within 3-sigma control limits, indicating a stable, controlled process. Results Outcome indicator Over the 32-week TPN QI initiative, the run chart with PDSA overlays ( ) showed progressive improvement in adherence from a baseline of ~10%, with a temporary drop to 0% in weeks 5 and 6 falling below the lower control limit, indicating special-cause variation related to a sepsis outbreak. Following corrective actions, adherence returned within 3-sigma limits and stabilised, with a mean of 84.2% across all weeks and 90.7% when weeks 5 and 6 were excluded. The p chart ( ) demonstrated a centreline shift from 66.0% in the early unstable phase to 94.1% in the stable phase, with values consistently trending towards the upper control limit and reduced common-cause variation , confirming sustained process improvement through sequential PDSA cycles. As a balancing outcome, the overall sepsis incidence among inborn neonates receiving TPN during the study period was 3.2%. Process indicators Environmental surveillance measures, including surface swabs, air quality monitoring with settle plates and periodic fumigation, were introduced from June 2024 following a sepsis outbreak. Although there were intermittent lapses, routine audits ensured that adherence to the surveillance protocol was maintained throughout the study period. Compliance with the QI intervention for TPN preparation and administration was 100% in all the months, with all preparations performed by trained residents/fellows using the standardised checklist under direct observation. Training participation ( ) improved progressively, with attendance rising from below 60% in May–June 2024 to 100% in later months, reflecting the effectiveness of structured, recurring training sessions in promoting protocol adherence. Discussion This QI project enhanced adherence to standardised TPN protocols in a high-volume Level III NICU by addressing preparation and administration gaps. Interventions included transitioning TPN preparation to trained residents and fellows, structured training, use of a TPN calculator, customised formulations and laminar flow surveillance, which became particularly critical following a sepsis outbreak. The systematic application of PDSA cycles enabled refinements, while the multidisciplinary approach supported integration into routine workflow. Several interventions were institutionalised as sustainable system-level changes, including adoption of a computerised prescription template to reduce transcription errors, daily use of the excel-based calculator, implementation of a structured laminar flow surveillance protocol with inclusion of this data in monthly departmental audit to ensure sustainability. The administration of PN is a multifaceted process requiring collaboration among various healthcare professionals, including dietitians, physicians, residents, pharmacists, nurses and compounding technicians. It involves a series of essential steps, starting from evaluating the patient’s nutritional needs to prescribing, transcribing, compounding, labelling and dispensing the formulation. Additionally, safe administration and continuous patient monitoring are crucial to ensure efficacy and prevent complications ( ). Low adherence to standardised TPN protocols is known to increase the risk of infection, metabolic instability, growth faltering and inadequate nutrient delivery, as highlighted in previous studies. In our project, we did not directly measure clinical outcomes such as CLABSI, electrolyte disturbances or growth; instead, our primary focus was protocol adherence. However, adherence is a well-recognised process measure and a validated surrogate for patient safety in TPN administration. By improving adherence through PDSA cycles, we aimed to reduce potential risks associated with inconsistent practices, even though outcome measures were not specifically tracked in this initiative. Over the past decades, various organisations have introduced guidelines and recommendations aimed at enhancing best practices, promoting standardisation and improving both safety and efficiency in PN administration. Sommer et al found that 14% of nurse-prepared PN formulations had dosing inaccuracies due to inadequate training and lack of aseptic protocols, advocating for centralised pharmacy preparation. In our initiative, improvement in adherence after transitioning TPN preparation to residents and fellows was not attributable to differences in discipline between cadres. Rather, the change reflected system modifications—structured training under neonatologist supervision, preparation in a dedicated laminar flow hood and use of an 11-step checklist with real-time monitoring. These measures reduced variability and errors that were common when preparation occurred ad hoc at the bedside. Standardised protocols and specialised training are crucial for ensuring safe and precise PN administration in neonatal care. The introduction of an Excel-based TPN calculator and a computerised prescription template led to automated complex calculations, reducing transcription and interpretation errors. Guenter et al emphasised that standardised competencies lower prescribing errors, while Kraft et al highlighted the role of pharmacist-led reviews in enhancing TPN safety. Despite established guidelines, errors persist—Krzyzaniak and Bajorek noted that administration errors account for 31%–63%, while dispensing errors (11.9%–25%) stem from labelling and formulation mistakes. A 2009 study reported PN prescription errors in 1.6% of cases, with transcription (39%), administration (35%) and preparation (24%) being the most common sources of error. Incident reports in 2010 identified PN and replacement preparations as major contributors to adverse drug events in paediatric patients (37% of cases), and a 2012 survey found that over 40% of institutions had not fully implemented safety safeguards. Even in a tertiary NICU, PN order errors were 3.9% in 2017 and in 2021, 0.6% of prescriptions still required intervention. These findings underscore the critical need for robust safety measures, pharmacist verification and institutional strategies to mitigate errors in neonatal TPN administration. Structured laminar flow surveillance played a vital role in preventing contamination-related complications, particularly following the sepsis outbreak. Stucki et al reported microbial contamination rates of 0% in cleanrooms, 6% in operating rooms and 16% in general wards, highlighting the necessity of controlled environments for PN preparation. These findings align with safety consensus recommendations, such as those by Ayers et al , emphasising rigorous infection control measures to ensure patient safety during PN administration. The training component was central to this QI initiative, evolving from comprehensive theoretical sessions, hands-on practical training and audio modules to refresher sessions and reading materials over time. The importance of sustained education is well supported in the literature—Mistry et al found that ongoing training significantly reduces patient safety incidents, while Ramakrishnan et al demonstrated that structured quality control minimises PN errors. Several of our PDSA interventions are also supported by published guidelines and evidence-based practices, making them potentially generalisable to other NICU settings. Standardised checklists and protocols are recommended by international PN safety guidelines. Transitioning preparation to trained residents and fellows aligns with evidence that inadequate training contributes to dosing inaccuracies. The use of computerised TPN calculators and order templates reflects established recommendations for standardised competencies and pharmacist-led reviews to reduce prescribing errors. Impact and future direction This QI project improved adherence to TPN protocols, streamlined preparation and enhanced safety practices in the NICU. While objective outcomes such as growth, infection rates and metabolic derangements were not assessed, these remain important areas for future evaluation to better understand the clinical impact of the intervention. Limitations The generalisability of this project is limited to NICUs with similar infrastructure, staffing and resource availability. Replication may be affected by variations in institutional protocols, staff training and infection control practices. Internal validity was constrained by the absence of a control group and potential confounders such as infection outbreaks and staffing changes. Data collection was based on observational audits and documentation, which may introduce reporting bias. Clinical outcomes such as CLABSI or dyselectrolytaemia were not systematically assessed, as the project was designed to target process improvement; overall sepsis incidence was reviewed only as a broad balancing measure. Financial evaluation was restricted to a crude comparison of consumable costs rather than formal cost-effectiveness analysis. Finally, no formal statistical testing was applied due to the real-time, iterative nature of QI cycles. Despite these limitations, structured audits, standardised protocols and continuous feedback contributed to the reliability and sustainability of the observed improvements. Conclusion This QI initiative effectively enhanced adherence to standardised TPN practices in a high-volume NICU through structured protocols, targeted training and process optimisation. The interventions improved preparation accuracy, minimised errors and promoted safer, more consistent TPN administration. These strategies offer a practical, replicable model for improving PN practices in similar neonatal care settings.
